data.title: TikTok misled consumers about filtering content for minors, judge rules
data.description:
A Texas judge on Thursday ruled the social media platform TikTok misled consumers about the company’s efforts to filter inappropriate content for minors.

In her ruling, Texas District Judge Cory Liu said TikTok’s claims about its content-moderation policies violated the Texas Deceptive Trade Practices Act.

The state of Texas alleged TikTok did not remove certain categories of videos, including sexually suggestive or graphic content or promotions of gambling or drugs, that violated the platform’s Community Guidelines.

The internal content-moderation policies, according the state, “instructed that such content should be allowed to remain on the platform with the designation of ‘hard to find’ rather than ‘do not allow,'” according to court filings.

The state also argued TikTok misled users when claiming its “Restricted Mode” effectively filtered out content potentially inappropriate for minors.

Prosecutors alleged TikTok employees internally acknowledged the restricted mode did not work as intended and “exposed users to a high amount of content that should have been filtered out,” the filing stated.

Liu ruled the state met the burden for summary judgement on both allegations, allowing the trial to move forward. The trial, which is expected to be set for next month, would mark the first full trial on safety claims for TikTok if a settlement is not reached beforehand.

Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton (R) celebrated Liu’s ruling Thursday, writing TikTok “sacrificed the safety and innocence of children for engagement and numbers, and now they are being held accountable.”

TikTok did not respond to request for comment.

TikTok is among a handful of social media companies to face increasing pressure rover its ability to protect children online.

The trial will follow two landmark verdicts earlier this year that found the social media giant Meta liable for its platforms’ impact on kids and teen mental and physical health.

Last month, Meta settled a similar case with nearly every state in the U.S., agreeing to pay more than $17 billion and roll out several platform changes. Texas was not part of this settlement, but revealed hours later it reached a separate agreement with Meta, bringing the company’s total sum to just over $18 billion.

In announcing the settlement, Meta specifically called out YouTube and TikTok to “join” the company in adopting what it calls a “new standard” for kids online safety. 

In an open letter, Meta argued the benefits of its new standards will only be “truly effective” if other industry players follow the same standard, putting public pressure on its rivals to make a deal. 

TikTok has largely stayed quiet, providing no public response on the letter.

data.title: George W. Bush shares painting of moment he learned of 9/11 attack
data.description:
Former President George W. Bush on Friday shared images of several paintings he created to mark the 25th anniversary of the Sept. 11, 2001, terrorist attacks. 

Bush, who was president on the tragic day, posted to social media his rendering of the moment his White House chief of staff, Andrew Card, notified him that the World Trade Center’s second tower had been hit and that “America is under attack.”

The artwork depicts Card leaning in to whisper the news to the president, who was participating in a lesson with children at an elementary school in Florida at the time. Bush wears a stunned expression in this image.

The piece is part of a larger exhibition of artwork the president created to mark the 25th anniversary of the day. The art will be on display at the George W. Bush Presidential Center in Dallas for the rest of the month.

“Twenty-five years ago, the actions of an enemy revealed the spirit of the American people,” Bush wrote on social media alongside images of the artwork. 

“May we always honor the precious lives stolen, and may God bless America,” he added. 

Other images included in this exhibit depict the plumes of smoke that rose from the New York City skyline after the towers were hit, the police badge of an officer killed in the attack and a giant American flag draped over the side of a building.

During a conversation at his presidential center with former Secretary of State Condoleezza Rice earlier this week, Bush reflected on the day he “became a wartime president.”

“There was no doubt in my mind that this was not a law enforcement event; this was a war,” Bush said. “And that the job of the president and the country and his team is to rally the nation to do what’s necessary to protect our people.”

Bush and all other former living U.S. presidents attended a memorial service at ground zero in New York City on Friday. President Trump spoke at a Pentagon ceremony on Friday marking the 25th anniversary of these attacks.

data.title: Health officials declare end to largest cyclospora outbreak in history
data.description:
The country’s largest outbreak of cyclospora illness has ended, federal health officials said Friday. 

The foodborne illness linked to contaminated lettuce sickened 12,883 people across 21 states, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, with more than 500 people hospitalized. Two people died in Michigan, which was the hardest-hit state, though health authorities said they had “significant underlying health conditions.”

The lettuce, supplied by Taylor Farms in Mexico, is no longer available in stores or restaurants. 

“At this time, there is no risk of people getting sick with cyclosporiasis from this source,” CDC wrote in the agency’s final update on the outbreak. 

Once federal officials began linking the illnesses to Taylor Farms lettuce in mid-July, the company voluntarily recalled products from the market. 

At the peak of the outbreak, before the recall, more than 1,000 infections occurred in a single day. Fewer than two infections per day on average occurred in August, CDC said. According to FDA, most of the illnesses tied to the outbreak began before the Taylor Farms iceberg lettuce recall was announced July 17. 

The CDC is still investigating several case clusters of the parasitic illness nationwide. Including the multi-state outbreak, CDC has received reports of 19,595 laboratory-confirmed cases of cyclosporiasis acquired in the United States. 

The Food and Drug Administration (FDA) said it is continuing its investigation into the outbreak, including how the product became contaminated with Cyclospora. Last month, the agency sent inspectors to the Taylor Farms processing center and lettuce farms in northeastern Mexico. 

In a letter to industry leaders, FDA’s acting deputy commissioner for food, Donald Prater, urged companies to invest more in cyclospora prevention and to follow food safety regulations. 

Cyclospora is a difficult parasite to track, and the incubation period of illness can take up to two weeks after food is consumed, meaning people are being asked to remember what they ate weeks earlier. Lettuce is also a highly perishable food, so by the time a potential source is identified, consumers have often either eaten or thrown away the affected product.

data.title: State lawmaker calls on Trump to rename Lake Erie as 'Lake Pennsylvania'
data.description:
Pennsylvania State Rep. David Maloney (R) called on President Trump this week to rename Lake Erie to “Lake Pennsylvania” following similar moves by the president earlier this year.

“This is Pennsylvania’s only Great Lake. Its modern economy and identity are increasingly tied to the boaters, anglers, families and tourists who come to enjoy it” Maloney said in a statement earlier this week. “Ohio has plenty of shoreline. New York already has two Great Lakes. Canada has four others.”

“Pennsylvania has one. Let’s call it Lake Pennsylvania,” he added.

Lake Erie is the smallest of the Great Lakes by volume and is also the shallowest, according to the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA). The lake has a total of 12 million people in its watershed, split between 10.5 million people in the U.S. and 1.9 million people in Canada.

In his announcement, Maloney called on Trump and the Department of Interior Secretary Doug Burgum to enforce the name change.

Trump signed an executive order formally changing the name of another Lake Ontario to “Lake America” amid the ongoing trade war with Canada. 

Canada’s retaliatory tariffs went into effect Tuesday with Pennsylvania expected to be heavily impacted by the 15, 25 and 50 percent tariffs on around 6 percent of what the U.S. exported to Canada last year.

Pennsylvania’s largest export market is Canada. In 2025, Pennsylvania exported $13.9 billion in goods to Canada, representing 27 percent of the state’s total goods exports, according to the U.S. Trade Representative’s Office.

The president has also proposed renaming New Mexico to “New America,” which initiated a negative response from several of the state’s Democratic lawmakers.

data.title: Savannah Guthrie opens up about mom, Nancy, ahead of Ireland trip
data.description:
(NewsNation) — Savannah Guthrie honored her mother, Nancy Guthrie, on Thursday during the “Today” show, sharing a personal connection to Ireland ahead of an upcoming trip with the morning show crew.

Guthrie revealed that the entire NBC team will travel to Ireland for a series of live broadcasts.

“I love that we’re all going. I’ve never been to Ireland,” she said. “My mother’s family — my mother was Irish, (as was) her grandmother. They were from Galway.”

The trip comes as the investigation into her mother’s disappearance continues.

Nancy Guthrie, 84, was believed to be abducted from her Tucson, Ariz., home in the early hours of Feb. 1, based on the time her pacemaker stopped communicating with her phone. She was reported missing the next day.

Authorities have said she likely was targeted before she was taken from her residence. She was last seen while being dropped off at home on Jan. 31 by a family member.

Since then, law enforcement has released security camera footage and multiple ransom notes, including one suggesting the NBC host’s mom is “buried with nature.”

Guthrie vowed that her family will “never stop looking for answers” about what happened to her mother.

data.title: Federal court rules against Trump order keeping Michigan coal plant running
data.description:
A federal appeals court on Friday struck down an order from the Trump administration keeping a Michigan coal plant open past its planned retirement.

The U.S. Court of Appeals for the D.C. Circuit ruled that the Energy Department went beyond its authority when it ordered J.H. Campbell Generating Plant in West Olive to remain open through at least the end of the summer after it was slated to shut down in May 2025.

The 64-year-old coal plant was set to close as part of a transition to cleaner energy after Consumers Energy spent years preparing to retire it. Michigan regulators and the regional grid operator had approved the plan.

Days before the plant was set to close, Energy Secretary Chris Wright ordered it to remain open, warning of possible electricity shortages and blackouts in the Midwest as summer demand increased.

“[The] emergency order ensures that Michiganders and the greater Midwest region do not lose critical power generation capability as summer begins and electricity demand regularly reach high levels,” Wright said in a statement announcing the order.

The order was challenged by Michigan officials, Illinois, Minnesota and several environmental groups, who sued the Trump administration to block the order.

The three-judge appeals court sided with the plaintiffs on Friday, finding that the Energy Department did not prove that there was a real emergency under federal law.

The emergency authority is “essentially a narrow, last-resort backstop,” Judge Cornelia Pillard, who was appointed by former President Obama, wrote for the unanimous panel.

The court said the power is meant for situations requiring immediate federal actions, not broader concerns about whether enough electricity will be available in the future.

The Associated Press found that the cost to keep the plant in Michigan operating beyond its May 2025 retirement reached roughly $259 million so far, citing new financial filings.

data.title: Trump administration announces first-ever deportation from terrorist removal court
data.description:
The Justice Department on Friday noted the removal of an Afghan woman in the first-ever Alien Terrorist Removal Court (ATRC) case, announcing the resolution on the anniversary of the 9/11 attacks although the woman was deported last month.

Nazira Haji Zada, a 47-year-old Afghan woman living in Fort Worth, Texas, was the first person to come before the previously dormant court.

Typically, the Justice Department seeks to convict and imprison those who are considered a terrorist threat rather than deport them. But in July they moved to deport Zada, whose sons were convicted in Oklahoma for their roles in a plot to carry out an attack on Election Day 2024. 

According to court filings unsealed Friday, Zada was deported on August 25 after she and her team of public defenders agreed she would be deported and accepted her designation as a terrorist, making her permanently barred from ever entering the U.S. again.

“This landmark case, resulting in the prompt removal of this alien terrorist to her country of origin, is a win for national security and the rule of law,” Attorney General Todd Blanche said in a statement. 

“Those who support and condone terrorism should not be living in the United States, and this first-ever case before the ATRC shows how the Department will use every tool at its disposal to protect our country.”

The Alien Terrorist Removal Court was established in 1996 but had never received a petition until July, when the Justice Department filed an application seeking Nazira’s removal.  

The case raised questions about the extent of Zada’s connection to ISIS, but the ATRC operates largely on classified information.

An unclassified summary unsealed on Friday accuses Zada of having “worked to indoctrinate her children with ISIS ideology and have them pledge loyalty to ISIS.” 

Zada is the mother and mother-in-law of two Afghan men who were convicted in Oklahoma for their roles in the 2024 Election Day plot. Her son, Abdullah Haji Zada, was sentenced in November to 15 years in prison, and court records show he previously agreed to be removed from the U.S. after he is released from prison. 

Her son-in-law, Nasir Ahmad Tawhedi, previously worked as a security guard for an American military installation in Afghanistan. He pleaded guilty to conspiring and attempting to provide material support to the Islamic State group, and prosecutors have said he took steps to advance his attack plans by ordering AK-47 rifles, liquidating his family’s assets and buying one-way tickets for his wife and child to travel home to Afghanistan.

data.title: Live updates: Trump, Vance, past presidents pause to remember Sept. 11
data.description:
President Trump and Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth remembered Sept. 11 at the Pentagon, while Vice President Vance joined past presidents and New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani (D) at Ground Zero on Friday morning, as America pauses to honor the victims of the 2001 terrorist attacks.

While the memorial in New York included no politics, remarks from Trump and Hegseth at the Pentagon memorial both raised the Iran conflict, tying the events together.

Twenty-five years after four jets took down the World Trade Center, crashed into the Pentagon and a field in Pennsylvania, the Trump administration is stepping gingerly into a loosening of tight airport security measures implemented in the aftermath.

The solemn day follows two days of cheerleading in Dallas for the Trump administration and Republican midterm candidates. Vance closed the convention amid growing chatter about his 2028 prospects. His Thursday night keynote offered the vice president a chance to charm the base that will be critical if he decides to run to succeed Trump in the next election.

The president returned to the White House before departing later Friday for Dublin. He’ll spend the weekend at his golf resort for the Irish Open.

data.title: Weight regain after diet pill use linked to rise in suicidal thoughts: Study
data.description:
(NewsNation) — People who used prescription weight loss medication and later regained the weight reported suicidal thoughts at more than four times the rate of people who never took the drugs, a new study found.

Researchers led by Dr. Son Ki-young, a family medicine professor at Asan Medical Center, analyzed data from 27,741 adults — 10,908 men and 16,833 women — who took part in a national health survey between 2013 and 2022.

Of those, 846 reported using prescription weight-loss drugs in the prior year, while 26,895 did not, according to the study published in Korean Journal of Family Practice.

Compared with people who hadn’t used the meds, those who had were 2.7 times more likely to report suicidal thoughts, 1.9 times more likely to report creating a plan and 1.7 times more likely to report an attempt.

They were also 1.9 times more likely to report depression lasting more than two weeks and twice as likely to have sought mental health counseling, the data shows.

The sharpest numbers came from a subgroup: people who took the medication and still gained weight.

Their odds of suicidal thoughts were 4.2 times higher than those who never used the drugs, while depression and counseling odds were roughly 1.9 and 1.8 times higher, the researchers found.

The study’s authors said the pattern likely reflects more than a direct drug effect.

“The increase in suicide-related index, among those who regained weight after weight-loss medication, is not just related to the neurological and psychiatric effects of the medicine itself,” the research team wrote, according to the International Business Times. “It is likely to be connected in a complex way to the psychological and social elements related to failing to control one’s weight.”

The study is observational, meaning it can’t prove the medications caused the mental health symptoms — only that a correlation exists.

The survey period also mostly predates widespread use of newer GLP-1 drugs like semaglutide (Wegovy) and tirzepatide (Zepbound, Mounjaro) in South Korea.

The sample instead largely reflects older appetite suppressants, including phentermine, diethylpropion, phendimetrazine, topiramate and orlistat — stimulant-based drugs already linked to anxiety, insomnia and mood changes.

People with severe obesity already have higher baseline rates of depression, anxiety and body-image distress and a one-time survey can’t separate preexisting symptoms from new ones.

In January, the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) asked drugmakers to remove suicidal-ideation warning language from the labels of Saxenda, Wegovy and Zepbound after a review of 91 placebo-controlled trials involving more than 107,000 patients found no increased risk of suicidal thoughts or behavior tied to GLP-1 drugs.

Novo Nordisk and Eli Lilly both said they support the FDA’s findings, though Lilly’s consumer materials still direct patients to watch for mood changes and contact a doctor if symptoms are “new, worse or worry you.”

data.title: Laura Ingraham presses Trump on $5,000 'bribe'
data.description:
Turns out, very few people were impressed by President Trump’s bribe attempt Wednesday night.  

If you missed it, here it is.

$5,000 to every American adult if Republicans win control of Congress. That estimated price tag is at least $1.3 trillion and would require congressional approval.  

One of the best critiques came from conservative National Review columnist Charles C.W. Cooke, who called Trump’s proposal “just preposterous.”  

He released an opinion piece saying: “Painfully aware that, once the midterms are over, he risks being gradually consigned to irrelevance, President Trump has hit once again upon a Hail Mary plan for political success. That plan is bribery.”  

He went on to say: “Last night, after vocally condemning the rise of socialism in the United States, Trump pledged some of his own.”  

The contradiction really is crazy. At the convention, Trump warned voters that Democrats are socialists who want to give away their money. Then he proposed giving Americans $5,000 each if Republicans win. For nothing else other than the fact that they won.  

If the policies are working, why is the sales pitch a check?  

The enhanced ACA premium tax credits expired at the end of 2025, increasing premiums for many Americans. Oil and gas prices have surged amid the ongoing Iran conflict, and tariffs remain a major part of the administration’s economic strategy while they hurt the average American consumer.  

So instead of explaining those policies and why Americans should stick with them, the message here seems to be: Here’s $5,000. Let me continue to make your life unaffordable.  

Even if you’re not upset about the fact that this sounded like a bribe, this is hardly the first promise of an erroneous payout that had absolutely no merit or chance of happening. CNN’s Manu Raju helped refresh our memory. 

The reality is, there is no $5,000 check getting approved by Congress, and federal law does prohibit offering payment for voting. So this is not happening.  

But between the tariffs, the Iran war and the mass deportation agenda that have all negatively affected our economy, this convention helped me realize that the Republican message is now: If you can’t beat ’em, bribe ’em. 

Lindsey Granger is a NewsNation contributor and co-host of The Hill’s commentary show “Rising.” This column is an edited transcription of her on-air commentary.
